1	# tally
     2	
     3	tally is a little command-line tool for keeping track of what you spend. It grew
     4	out of a spreadsheet that got out of hand, and honestly it still carries a bit of
     5	that spreadsheet energy — you throw expenses at it, and it adds them up for you by
     6	month and by category. There is no server, no account, no sync. Everything lives
     7	in a single JSON file next to wherever you run it, which means you can back it up,
     8	diff it, or just delete it and start over whenever the mood strikes.
     9	
    10	The idea is that recording an expense should take about as long as it takes to
    11	think of it. You type the amount, a category, maybe a note, and you are done. Later,
    12	when you want to know where the money went, you ask for a report.
    13	
    14	## Installing
    15	
    16	There is nothing to install beyond Python 3.9 or newer. Clone the repository and
    17	run it as a module:
    18	
    19	```
    20	python -m tally.cli --help
    21	```
    22	
    23	If you like, drop a shell alias so you can just type `tally`.
    24	
    25	## Recording an expense
    26	
    27	```
    28	python -m tally.cli add 12.50 food --note "lunch"
    29	```
    30	
    31	The first two arguments are the amount and the category. By default the amount is
    32	read as US dollars, but you can enter it in another currency and tally will convert
    33	it for you:
    34	
    35	```
    36	python -m tally.cli add 39 food --currency EUR --date 2024-03-04
    37	```
    38	
    39	If you leave off `--date`, today's date is used.
    40	
    41	## Looking at your spending
    42	
    43	The `report` command prints category totals for a month. You can narrow it to a
    44	single category too:
    45	
    46	```
    47	python -m tally.cli report --month 2024-03
    48	python -m tally.cli report --month 2024-03 --category food
    49	```
    50	
    51	There is also a `list` command if you would rather see the individual expenses
    52	instead of the totals, and an `export` command that writes everything out as CSV
    53	so you can open it in a spreadsheet after all:
    54	
    55	```
    56	python -m tally.cli list --month 2024-03
    57	python -m tally.cli export --out march.csv
    58	```
    59	
    60	## How amounts are stored
    61	
    62	Whenever you add an expense, tally converts the amount into US dollars using the
    63	conversion table in `tally/rates.py` and stores that dollar figure. The original
    64	amount and currency you typed are kept alongside it for reference, but every total
    65	you ever see is computed in US dollars. This keeps reports consistent even when a
    66	month mixes several currencies.
    67	
    68	## A note on scope
    69	
    70	This is a personal tool, not an accounting package. It does not do tax categories,
    71	receipts, shared budgets, or anything clever with recurring expenses. If you need
    72	those, you have outgrown tally. If you just want to know whether you spent too much
    73	on takeout last month, you are in the right place.
---
     1	# Contributing to tally
     2	
     3	Thanks for taking a look. tally is deliberately small, and the goal is to keep it
     4	that way. A few conventions keep the codebase easy to reason about.
     5	
     6	## Dependencies
     7	
     8	**tally depends on the Python standard library and pytest, and nothing else.**
     9	Runtime code (everything under `tally/`) must import only from the standard library.
    10	Do not add third-party runtime dependencies — no requests, no dateutil, no click,
    11	no pandas. If you find yourself reaching for a library, that is usually a sign the
    12	feature belongs outside tally. pytest is the only permitted dependency, and it is
    13	used exclusively by the test suite.
    14	
    15	This rule is not negotiable in a pull request; a change that adds a dependency will
    16	be sent back regardless of how nice the library is.
    17	
    18	## Style
    19	
    20	- Target Python 3.9. Do not use syntax newer than 3.9 (no structural pattern
    21	  matching, no `X | Y` union type hints — use `typing.Optional` / `typing.Union`).
    22	- Functions and variables use `snake_case`; constants use `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`.
    23	- Keep functions small and single-purpose. If a function needs a paragraph to
    24	  explain, it probably wants to be two functions.
    25	- Every public function gets a one-line docstring at minimum.
    26	
    27	## Tests
    28	
    29	- Every behavioural change comes with a test.
    30	- The suite must stay green: `python -m pytest` with zero failures and zero
    31	  warnings before you open a pull request.
    32	- Tests that pin specific numbers (currency conversions, rounding, totals) are
    33	  there on purpose. If a change makes one fail, understand why before you touch
    34	  the test — the failing test may be the point.
    35	
    36	## Commits
    37	
    38	Small, focused commits with a present-tense summary line. One logical change per
    39	commit where you can manage it.
---
     1	# tally — Frequently Asked Questions
     2	
     3	## Is tally really free?
     4	
     5	Yes. Running tally on your own computer is free and always will be. The only thing
     6	that costs money is the optional hosted backup add-on.
     7	
     8	## How many expenses can I track on the free plan?
     9	
    10	The free plan includes hosted backup for up to **100 expenses per month**. You can
    11	record more than that locally — nothing stops you — but only the first 100 in a
    12	month are covered by the free backup. The Plus and Family plans remove the limit.
    13	
    14	## Where is my data kept?
    15	
    16	In a single JSON file on your own machine. Unless you turn on the hosted backup
    17	add-on, your data never leaves your computer.
    18	
    19	## Can I enter expenses in other currencies?
    20	
    21	Yes. Pass `--currency` when you add an expense and tally converts it to US dollars
    22	for you.
---
     1	# tally — Product Requirements
     2	
     3	This document records the behaviour tally is expected to have. It is the reference
     4	of record: where the code, the README, or the marketing copy disagree with this
     5	document, this document wins until it is deliberately changed.
     6	
     7	## R1 — Single-file store
     8	
     9	All data lives in one JSON file. There is no database and no network access. The
    10	store file records a schema version so older files can be migrated forward.
    11	
    12	## R2 — Amounts are normalized to US dollars at write time
    13	
    14	Every expense amount is converted to US dollars **when it is recorded**, using the
    15	conversion table in `tally/rates.py`, and the US-dollar figure is what gets stored.
    16	The original amount and currency the user entered are retained for reference only;
    17	they are never used to compute a total.
    18	
    19	The consequence, which is intentional: every total, summary, budget comparison, and
    20	export is denominated in US dollars. tally does not re-convert into another currency
    21	at report time. A report that mixed stored dollars with re-converted originals would
    22	double-count the conversion and is a defect.
    23	
    24	## R3 — Conversion rates are fixed constants
    25	
    26	The rates in `tally/rates.py` are treated as fixed. Several tests pin totals that
    27	are computed from them. Changing a rate is allowed, but it is a deliberate act: the
    28	pinned expectations must be updated in the same change, and the change should be
    29	called out because it alters every historical total that used that currency.
    30	
    31	## R4 — Categories
    32	
    33	Expenses are filed under a category. The set of known categories and their monthly
    34	budgets live in `tally/config.py`.
    35	
    36	## R5 — Reporting
    37	
    38	tally reports category totals for a month, can filter to a single category, can list
    39	individual expenses, and can export the full set to CSV. The CSV export is
    40	denominated in US dollars, consistent with R2.
    41	
    42	## R6 — Documentation consistency
    43	
    44	The customer-facing documents must not contradict each other on published limits.
    45	In particular, `docs/pricing.md` and `docs/faq.md` both state the free-tier expense
    46	limit, and **the two must always agree**. A change to a published limit in one file
    47	is incomplete until the other file is updated to match.
